subject: Negative variance of an observed variable

messages.author: c8b4e2dc3565b448
messages.subject: Negative variance of an observed variable
parts:
I am fitting a model with 12 manifest variables on 3 first order factors and one second order factor. I get negative variances estimated for one latent variable (first order factor), and one observed variable. In LISREL I could just set these variances to a small positive quantity (say 0.001), but when I try this in lavaan it works for the latent variable but not the observed variable. The observed variable is still estimated, my constraints on its value are ignored.
Is this because lavaan will not allow me to specify the value of the variance of an observed variable, or do I need to specify the value for this variance using syntax other than "x~~0.001*x".

Help
Graeme Tucker

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Negative variance of an observed variable
parts:
That syntax should work fine, assuming your observed variable is continuous.  If your observed indicator is ordinal, you need to set parameterization="theta" to make residual variances model parameters.  But constraining variances to be positive is not necessarily a good solution.  It can bias other estimates, and your model-fit test statistic will no longer be distributed as a chi-squared random variable.  Fixing variances to force a solution to be "admissible" is old advice based on the fallacious confusion between variance parameters (which surely cannot be negative) and statistics (which merely estimate parameters).  Assuming your model fits reasonably well, sampling error is a more probable explanation for Heywood cases.  How large is your sample?  Using summary(fit, ci = TRUE), do the 95% CIs include positive values?  

https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0049124112442138

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Negative variance of an observed variable
parts: The observed indicator is ordinal, so I don't yet have a confidence interval.

Ah right, because it is not an estimate.  Well, if you set std.lv=TRUE and use the default parameterization="delta", then the loadings will already be standardized.  In that case (assuming simple structure), a negative residual variance would occur if and only if your standardized loading exceeds +/- 1.  So you can check that CI to verify that it includes admissible values, which has the same implications for your model-implied residual variance.
